title: Scales and Keys
intro: A scale is a set of pitches arranged in order within an octave. The major scale, with its fixed pattern of whole and half steps, is the reference point for naming intervals, chords and keys in tonal music.

blocks.text: Play the white keys from C to C and you hear the major scale. Its steps follow the pattern whole–whole–half–whole–whole–whole–half (W W H W W W H). Any note can start a major scale as long as that pattern is kept; sharps or flats fix the steps that the white keys get wrong.

To build D major: start on D and apply W W H W W W H. D→E (W), E→F♯ (W, so F must be sharpened), F♯→G (H), G→A, A→B (W W), B→C♯ (W, so C is sharpened), C♯→D (H). Each letter appears exactly once, which is why the third note is F♯ and not G♭.
Each note of a scale has a number (with a caret, 1̂ to 7̂) and a name describing its role:

items: 1̂ tonic: home, the note the key is named after.
2̂ supertonic · 3̂ mediant (halfway from tonic to dominant) · 4̂ subdominant (a fifth below the tonic).
5̂ dominant: a fifth above the tonic; the strongest pull back to it.
6̂ submediant (halfway down to the subdominant) · 7̂ leading tone: a semitone below the tonic, pulling up to it. (In natural minor, where 7̂ is a whole step below, it is called the subtonic.)

blocks.text: Tendency tones give tonal music its sense of motion: 7̂ wants to rise to 1̂, 4̂ wants to fall to 3̂, and 2̂ moves to 1̂ or 3̂. The two half steps of the major scale (3̂–4̂ and 7̂–1̂) are where that pull is strongest.

A key is the tonal centre a piece is organised around plus the scale it mainly uses. A piece in G major treats G as home and uses F♯ throughout. The key signature collects the sharps or flats of the scale at the start of each line, so they need not be written on every note.

Scale fingering lets the hand pass smoothly along the keyboard: the thumb passes under after finger 3 or 4, and the thumb never plays a black key. For C, G, D, A and E major the right hand plays 1 2 3 1 2 3 4 5 going up (thumb under after the third note); the left hand plays 5 4 3 2 1 3 2 1 (finger 3 crosses over after the thumb). F major's right hand is 1 2 3 4 1 2 3 4 so the thumb avoids B♭. Scales starting on black keys put the thumb on the first white key after the black group.

items: Step 1. Right hand, C major from middle C: thumb (1) on C, 2 on D, 3 on E, then pass the thumb under to play F, then 2 on G, 3 on A, 4 on B, 5 on C. Fingering 1 2 3 1 2 3 4 5.
Step 2. Coming down: 5 4 3 2 1 on C B A G F, then cross finger 3 over the thumb to play E, and 2 1 on D C.
Step 3. Left hand, C major from the C below: 5 4 3 2 1 on C D E F G, then cross 3 over the thumb to A, 2 on B, 1 on C.
Step 4. Now G major: same fingering from G, but play F♯ (the black key) instead of F. Then F major: B♭ instead of B, with right-hand fingering 1 2 3 4 1 2 3 4 so the thumb avoids the black key.
Step 5. Build D major with the whole-whole-half pattern by counting keys from D: you will find F♯ and C♯. Step through the D major example above to check.

blocks.title: Build a scale
solution: Start on E♭ and apply W W H W W W H: E♭–F (W), F–G (W), G–A♭ (H), A♭–B♭ (W), B♭–C (W), C–D (W), D–E♭ (H). Flats: B♭, E♭, A♭.
blocks.answer: E♭ F G A♭ B♭ C D E♭

blocks.title: Degree names
blocks.text: In A major, which note is the leading tone, and which is the subdominant?
solution: A major is A B C♯ D E F♯ G♯. The leading tone (7̂) is G♯; the subdominant (4̂) is D.
